title: Why Is Cannabis Microdosing So Popular? 7 Reasons
h1: Why Microdosing Cannabis Keeps Gaining Fans: Seven Reasons

body:
Cannabis microdosing means taking a very small amount of THC, enough for a subtle shift or sometimes nothing noticeable, instead of aiming for a strong high. It has drawn more attention as legal markets made measured doses easy to find. Here's what counts as a microdose, seven reasons it keeps gaining fans and what research does and doesn't show yet. This is educational information for adults 21 and older, not medical advice.

## What counts as a microdose

There's no official definition. Researchers at the University of California San Diego and Stanford describe microdosing as taking about one-fifth to one-twentieth of a typical recreational dose. In Michigan, one adult-use edible serving can contain up to 10 mg of THC. Measured against that, a microdose works out to roughly 0.5 to 2 mg.

Some people go a little lower or higher. What matters is that the dose is small, measured and consistent, so you can tell how it affects you.

## Reason 1: staying functional

Some adults want cannabis to fit into a regular day rather than take it over, and lab research shows why smaller doses appeal: effects grow with the dose. In a Johns Hopkins study of healthy adults who rarely used cannabis, a 10 mg THC brownie produced noticeable effects and a faster heart rate but didn't measurably impair thinking or coordination. Doses of 25 and 50 mg markedly impaired both.

Smaller doses mean milder effects, but any amount of THC can affect you. Never drive or operate machinery after using cannabis.

## Reason 2: an easier first step for new consumers

For newcomers, a small dose is a lower-stakes way to learn how cannabis feels. That matters most with edibles. In the same study, effects didn't show up for 30 to 60 minutes and peaked 1.5 to 3 hours after eating.

Starting small and waiting before taking more helps you avoid the classic mistake of doubling up too soon. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) covers serving sizes in detail.

## Reason 3: precise low-dose products

Legal products make small doses easier to measure. In Michigan, adult-use edibles are capped at 10 mg of THC per serving and 200 mg per package. Labels list THC and CBD content, with a note that actual values may vary by 10%.

That makes the math simple. Cut a 10 mg piece into quarters and each quarter holds about 2.5 mg, and some products come in smaller servings to begin with. Tinctures with marked droppers and drinks with clear per-serving amounts work too. Products that pair THC with CBD in set ratios are another option, and our [cannabinoid ratios guide](/blog/cannabinoid-ratios-guide/) explains how to read those labels.

## Reason 4: it fits daily routines

A small, predictable amount is easier to plan around. Some adults enjoy one on a quiet evening or a weekend afternoon at home instead of saving cannabis for a big night.

A steady routine also makes it easier to notice how a given amount affects you. Keep a simple log of the product, the amount and the timing so you can adjust with care.

## Reason 5: part of wider self-care habits

For some adults, a measured dose fits a broader habit of paying closer attention to what they consume. In a 2023 national survey of 1,523 adults, people who had microdosed cannabis most often gave reasons they described as medical.

Reasons aren't results, though. The survey asked why people microdosed, not whether it did anything for them.

## Reason 6: less stigma, more education

Legal stores, clear labels and budtenders who can explain a serving size have made cannabis less mysterious. The same 2023 survey found microdosing was more common among people living in places with fewer restrictions on cannabis and psychedelics.

Michigan's licensed market is part of that shift. Products carry state-required labels and warnings, and stores check ID before every sale.

## Reason 7: cannabis microdosing research is growing but early

Interest is growing faster than the science. Most of what we know comes from lab studies of single doses and from surveys:

- **More isn't always better.** In a University of Chicago study of 42 healthy adults, 7.5 mg of THC was linked to lower self-reported distress after a stressful public-speaking task. A 12.5 mg dose increased negative mood. It was a small lab study, and it doesn't show that microdosing helps any health condition.
- **Tolerance builds.** A 2018 systematic review of human research found that regular cannabis use blunts many of THC's effects over time, especially on thinking and memory.
- **Surveys show links, not causes.** Microdosing was more common among people who reported poorer mental health. That doesn't mean microdosing caused it, or that it helped.

Until larger studies arrive, be skeptical of any claim that microdosing is proven to do something.

## Trying it responsibly in Michigan

- **Be 21 or older,** or a registered medical patient 18 or older, and buy from a licensed store.
- **Start with the smallest amount** you can measure, and keep it consistent.
- **Wait before taking more.** Edibles can take up to three hours to peak.
- **Skip the mix.** Don't combine cannabis with alcohol or other substances.
- **Don't drive** or operate a boat after using cannabis.
- **Store it safely,** locked up and away from kids and pets.
- **Talk with a clinician** if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, take medications or have a health condition.
- **Take breaks.** If a small dose starts doing less, consider a pause; our guide to [tolerance breaks](/blog/t-breaks-marijuana-tolerance/) explains how.

For step-by-step how-tos, read our guide to [microdosing THC and CBD](/blog/microdosing-marijuana-thc-cbd/). If you have questions about reading a label, our budtenders at [High Society's Michigan stores](/dispensary-locations/) are happy to help, though they can't give medical advice.

faq.q: What is a microdose of THC?
faq.a: There's no official amount. Researchers describe microdosing as taking about one-fifth to one-twentieth of a typical recreational dose. Measured against a 10 mg Michigan edible serving, that's roughly 0.5 to 2 mg of THC. Start at the low end and keep the amount consistent so you can tell how it affects you.

Sometimes. At very low doses, some people notice a subtle change and others notice nothing at all, and sensitivity varies from person to person. Your tolerance, what you've eaten and the product all play a part. With edibles, wait the full onset time, up to three hours to peak, before deciding whether to adjust.

Smaller doses generally mean milder effects, but no dose is right for everyone. THC can still affect coordination, reaction time and mood, and it can interact with medications. Don't drive after using it. If you're pregnant or breastfeeding, take medications or have a health condition, talk with a clinician before you try it.

Products with clearly measured servings. Low-dose edibles, tinctures with marked droppers and drinks with clear per-serving amounts all help, and you can split a standard 10 mg serving into smaller pieces. Inhaled cannabis is harder to measure precisely. Selection varies by store, so ask your budtender about low-dose options.

It can. A 2018 systematic review concluded that regular cannabis use blunts many of THC's effects over time. Little research has looked at microdosing specifically, but regular use of any amount may build some tolerance. If a small dose starts doing less, consider a short break rather than a bigger dose.

claims.claim: Researchers at UC San Diego and Stanford describe microdosing as about one-fifth to one-twentieth of a typical recreational dose.
claims.evidence: Abstract via E-utilities (Am J Prev Med 2026; UCSD and Stanford affiliations): "Microdosing involves consuming low doses of psychoactive substances, typically between 1/5th and 1/20th of a recreational dose."

claims.claim: Against a 10 mg Michigan edible serving, a microdose is roughly 0.5 to 2 mg of THC.
claims.evidence: 10 mg / 20 = 0.5 mg; 10 mg / 5 = 2 mg; framed as measured against the 10 mg serving cap, not as a standard dose.

claims.claim: Michigan adult-use edibles are capped at 10 mg THC per serving and 200 mg per package.
claims.evidence: "Adult-use edibles in Michigan are capped at 10 mg THC per dose and 200 mg per package".

claims.claim: Michigan labels list THC and CBD content with a note that actual values may vary by 10%.
claims.evidence: "THC and CBD concentration with a statement that actual values may vary by 10%".

claims.claim: In a 2023 national survey of 1,523 adults, 9.4% of U.S. adults said they had microdosed cannabis at some point.
claims.evidence: "survey ... of 1,523 U.S. adults was conducted in October-November 2023"; "Cannabis was the most commonly microdosed substance (9.4%; 95% CI=8.0, 10.7; 24.1 million adults)"; lifetime prevalence.

claims.claim: People who had microdosed cannabis most often gave reasons they described as medical; the survey asked reasons, not results.
claims.evidence: "Cannabis (41.2%; 95% CI=33.3, 49.5) was primarily microdosed for medical purposes" (the plurality reason); the article names no condition and adds "Reasons aren't results".

claims.claim: Microdosing was more common among people in places with fewer restrictions on cannabis and psychedelics, and among people reporting poorer mental health (association, not cause).
claims.evidence: "lifetime microdose use was more prevalent among respondents reporting poorer mental health and among those residing in jurisdictions that permitted recreational cannabis use and had decriminalized psychedelic possession".

claims.claim: Johns Hopkins study of healthy adults who rarely used cannabis: a 10 mg THC brownie produced noticeable effects and a faster heart rate without measurably impairing thinking or coordination; 25 and 50 mg markedly impaired both.
claims.evidence: Abstract (PMID 32298998): Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit; 17 adults abstinent 60+ days; "the 10 mg THC dose produced discriminable subjective drug effects and elevated heart rate but did not alter cognitive/psychomotor performance. The 25 and 50 mg THC doses ... markedly impaired cognitive and psychomotor functioning".

claims.claim: Edible effects didn't show for 30 to 60 minutes and peaked 1.5 to 3 hours after eating; edibles can take up to three hours to peak.
claims.evidence: "pharmacodynamic effects did not manifest until 30-60 min after ingestion, and peak effects occurred 1.5-3 h post-administration".

claims.claim: Lab research shows THC's effects grow with the dose.
claims.evidence: "Ingestion of oral cannabis dose-dependently altered subjective drug effects and impaired cognitive performance."

claims.claim: University of Chicago study of 42 healthy adults: 7.5 mg THC was linked to lower self-reported distress after a stressful public-speaking task; 12.5 mg increased negative mood; small lab study, no health benefit shown.
claims.evidence: Abstract (PMID 28599212): "Healthy volunteers (N=42)"; "7.5mg THC significantly reduced self-reported subjective distress after the TSST"; "12.5mg THC increased negative mood overall". The article states it does not show microdosing helps any health condition.

claims.claim: A 2018 systematic review found regular cannabis use blunts many of THC's effects over time, especially on thinking and memory.
claims.evidence: "acute effects of single cannabinoid administration are less prominent in regular cannabis users"; "Cognitive function is the domain showing the highest degree of tolerance"; intoxicating and cardiac effects "also blunted ... but to a lesser extent".

claims.claim: FAQ: "daily use of any amount adds up" (tolerance).
claims.fix: The review covers regular users in general, not microdoses, so tolerance at any amount is not shown. Softened to "regular use of any amount may build some tolerance".
claims.evidence: Review compares regular with non-regular users and repeated administration; no microdose-specific data.

claims.claim: Little research has looked at microdosing specifically.
Cutting a 10 mg piece into quarters gives about 2.5 mg each.
Michigan products carry state-required labels and warnings, and stores check ID before every sale.
claims.evidence: Required warnings under R 420.504(1); "Before any sale the store must check a valid driver's license or government-issued photo ID".

claims.claim: THC can affect coordination, reaction time and mood and can interact with medications; inhaled cannabis is harder to measure precisely.
claims.evidence: Psychomotor impairment at higher doses (Schlienz 2020); mood effects (Childs 2017). The medication-interaction line is a general caution paired with 'talk with a clinician'.

claims.claim: Adults 21+, or registered medical patients 18+, may buy from licensed stores; budtenders can help read labels but can't give medical advice.
claims.evidence: "Recreational shopping is available to individuals 21 years or older."; "Individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases." Link goes to /dispensary-locations/ only, as the medical rule allows.

claims.claim: Medical-article compliance: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links; no ordering section; no claim that microdosing treats anxiety, depression, pain or ADHD; no dose called safe for everyone; clinician advice for pregnancy, medications and conditions.

claims.evidence: Internal links: four blog guides and /dispensary-locations/; the brief's suggested /shop/ link is correctly absent; FAQ says "no dose is right for everyone".

review.notes: Writer's note kept: medical-risk article with no shop, menu, deals or rewards links and no shopping section; /dispensary-locations/ only for label questions; no treatment claims; no brand names. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 19 claims checked, 1 fixed (tolerance line softened). Sources list unchanged (6): four studies read through NCBI E-utilities plus two CRA documents listed in law-facts.
